new_statements.quote: The length is not phonemic. However, the long vocoids occur in the phonetic level and their occurrences are predictable. The vocoids occurring in the mono- syllabic words are uniformly long; while in disyllabic, tri – syllabic and tetra- syllabic words (available a very few), the vocoids of the second syllable are long. Stress also is a co- occurring feature with the length, i.e., the syllables having long vocoids are always stressed.

It sits in section 2.3 "Major allophonics distributions" of the Nagpuria sketch (also at line 22803-22808 of). The sibling paragra…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and rides on predictable phonetic vowel length: a monosyllable is long and stressed; in words of two or more syllables the vowel of the second syllable is long and therefore stressed. The section's own transcriptions mark stress on the second syllable of polysyllables ([imá:n] 'honesty', [kirá:] 'worm', [kAtá:ri] 'sugarcane', [geRé:] 'duck', [gA:dé:la] 'issueless cow').
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in the Nagpuria sketch. The sibling sketch in the same volume (Ghosh & Pattanaik, 'Sadan/Sadri', printed p. 652 = PDF p. 669, same file) gives a different conditioning: 'Length is not phonemic in Sadan/Sadri. Phonetically lengths of vowels are predictable only in the close syllable. Stress: Stress is not phonemic in Sadan/Sadri. It occurs mainly with long vowels in the close syllable.' Both agree stress is non-phonemic and length-linked; they disagree on whether length (hence stress) goes to the second syllable or to closed syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in a phoneme/allophone inventory); nothing on phrase-level prominence. Stress is treated as a phonetic correlate of predictable length, not as an independent prosodic system; the sketch is a government survey description (fieldwork Ranchi and Palamau districts 1978-80, updated 2010), not an instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from the 'Nagpuria' mother-tongue sketch (Srivastava & Pattanaik 2023; fieldwork Ranchi and Palamau districts), i.e. Chotanagpuri Sadri/Nagpuri of the Ranchi plateau, which Glottolog lists under sadr1248 (alternate names Nagpuri, Chota Nagpuri, Sadani). The same 2023 volume carries a separate census-label sketch 'Sadan/Sadri' (Ghosh & Pattanaik, Ranchi district) with a differing conditioning of stress, quoted under exceptions. Uranw & Yadav 2009 describe the Kisaan 'Saadri' of Jhapa, Nepal, a diaspora variety, and are silent on stress. Assam tea-garden Sadri (Saikia 2015, Dey 2011) is not represented in the opened sources.

sources.locator: Section 2.3 'Major allophonics distributions', printed p. 459 (PDF p. 476 of the 1002-page scan)
sources.note: Length not phonemic but predictable: monosyllables long; in di-/tri-/tetrasyllables the vowel of the second syllable is long; 'Stress also is a co-occurring feature with the length, i.e., the syllables having long vocoids are always stressed' (p. 459). Allophone examples carry the stress mark on the second syllable of polysyllables ([imá:n], [kirá:], [kAtá:ri], [geRé:], [gA:dé:la]).

sources.citation: Grierson, G.A. 1903. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. V Part II: Indo-Aryan family, Eastern group (Bihari and Oriya). Calcutta. 'Nagpuria or Sadan', pp. 277 ff.
sources.note: The Nagpuria/Sadan section (p. 277 ff.) describes classification, geography and specimens; no accent statement. The only accent rule in the volume is Bihari-general, under the Maithili introduction p. 24: 'the general rule is to throw it back as far as possible... The accent cannot be thrown further back than the antepenultimate, and if the penultimate is long the accent falls on it.' Not specific to Sadri.
